title: 1 g of black pepper in breakfast: what blood glucose did over the next 3 hours [meals, nothing_else]
teaser: Twenty healthy adults ate the same egg-and-toast breakfast four ways. [sample, meals] With 1 g of black pepper in the egg, blood glucose was lower 30 minutes later. [in_egg, glucose_lower, glucose_30] Added up over 3 hours, the meals did not differ. [glucose_total, nothing_else]
hook: 1 g of black pepper in a breakfast egg, and blood glucose was lower 30 minutes later. [in_egg, glucose_lower, glucose_30] Added up over the full 3 hours, there was no difference. [glucose_total, nothing_else]
populationPanel: Who this was tested in: 20 healthy adults, 10 men and 10 women. [sample] The women averaged 21.4 years old and the men 21.9. [ages] The entry rules asked for a body mass index of 18.5 to 24.9 and no chronic disease. [criteria] Each person ate all four breakfasts in randomized order, a week apart. [crossover, washout] The result describes one meal in people like these. [single_meal, sample] It says nothing about diabetes or any other disease. [criteria]

paragraphs: Think of a doorbell in your mouth. [-] Food presses it, and the rest of the body hears that a meal is on the way. [-] The authors point to a real one: a sensor in the mouth called TRPV1. [trpv1_mouth] Black pepper carries a compound called piperine and several close relatives. [piperine, trpv1] The authors say these might press that sensor. [trpv1]

What happens next is a hormone. [-] When TRPV1 fires, levels of a gut hormone called GLP-1 go up in the lower gut and in the blood. [glp1] GLP-1 is the gut's message that food has arrived. [glp1, concept:glucagon-like-peptide] It helps hold down the rise in blood sugar after eating, slows the gut and curbs appetite. [concept:glucagon-like-peptide]

That chain fits what the trial saw. [-] After the pepper breakfast, blood glucose was lower than after the plain one. [glucose_lower] The gap showed at the 30-minute reading. [glucose_30] Hunger was lower too. [appetite]
Turmeric did not follow the script. [-] On its own, 1 g did nothing to blood glucose. [turmeric_none] The authors' explanation is the dose: they call it low. [turmeric_dose]

figure.caption: The authors' explanation, step by step. [trpv1, glp1] A dashed arrow is a step the trial did not measure. [lim_hormones]
figure.alt: Four boxes, top to bottom, joined by dashed arrows. [-] Pepper touches the mouth. [-] A sensor there fires. [-] The gut sends its food-has-arrived message. [-] Blood sugar rises less. [-] Only the last box is filled. [-]

paragraphs: The trial tested one dose: 1 g of black pepper, mixed into a fried egg. [in_egg] The egg came with 2 slices of toast and a cup of sweet milk tea. [plate] The participants ate after an overnight fast and finished within 10 minutes. [fast, eaten_in]

A second version added 1 g of turmeric to the pepper. [meals] It showed the same early glucose difference, and tasters liked it more than pepper alone. [glucose_30, taste_rank] Turmeric without pepper showed no glucose effect. [turmeric_none]
Each version was eaten once. [single_meal, washout] The trial did not test a daily habit. [lim_long_term]

figure.caption: Each dot is one reading. [timepoints] Orange marks the readings that differed from the plain meal. [glucose_30]
figure.alt: Four rows of five dots, one row for each meal. [-] The readings were at 0, 30, 60, 120 and 180 minutes. [timepoints] At 30 minutes, the pepper meal and the both-spices meal are marked as differing from the plain meal. [glucose_30] A bracket over all five readings says the total showed no difference. [glucose_total]

audit.effect: The paper's text gives no size for the glucose difference. [glucose_30] It says only that the two pepper meals differed from the plain meal at 30 minutes, with p = .023. [glucose_30]
audit.weakEnd: The paper reports no confidence interval for any glucose result. [glucose_30] The gap could be wide or barely there; the text cannot say. [glucose_30] Over the full 3 hours, total blood glucose did not differ between the four meals. [glucose_total, nothing_else]
limitations: The trial measured no hormones. [lim_hormones] The sensor-and-hormone story is the authors' idea, not a result. [lim_hormones, lim_mechanism]
Hunger and fullness were self-reported on paper scales. [appetite_scale] The authors say the lower hunger might come from the spiced meals tasting worse. [lim_taste]
One breakfast per version, in 20 young adults: nothing here speaks to long-term use. [single_meal, sample, ages, lim_long_term]
audit.missed: The easy summary: these spices are good for blood sugar. [-] The paper found no glucose effect for turmeric alone. [turmeric_none] The 3-hour total did not differ for any meal. [glucose_total, nothing_else] Only healthy people took part, so the trial cannot speak to diabetes. [criteria, sample]
more: The paper does not say whether the participants knew which meal they had. [-]
The ingredient table lists 10 g of sugar for the combined meal and 8 g for the others. [sugar_row] It still gives all four the same 50 g of carbohydrate. [carb_row]
Overall taste scores out of 9: plain 6.5, pepper 6.2, turmeric 6.1, both spices 6.6. [taste_scale, taste_c, taste_bp, taste_tr, taste_both]
Stomach and gut symptoms, also self-rated, did not differ between meals. [gut, gut_scale]
The authors name one weakness: they never measured the meals' glycemic index. [lim_stated]

glossary.plain: Chance decided the order of the meals, not the people running the trial.
A sensor found in the mouth.
The main active ingredient of black pepper.
The sugar carried in the blood, measured here from a finger prick.

takeaways: The dose tested was 1 g of black pepper, cooked into the egg of a toast-and-tea breakfast. [in_egg, plate]
The glucose difference showed 30 minutes after eating and not in the 3-hour total. [glucose_30, glucose_total, nothing_else]
Turmeric alone, at 1 g, showed no glucose effect. [turmeric_none]
